opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question, and I think the first thing is to be honest that the uncertainty is real. It's tempting to pick a confident story, whether utopian or catastrophic, because certainty feels better than not knowing. But a lot of the people I respect most in this field have been surprised again and again by what these systems can do and how quickly things have moved. So humility seems like the right starting point.

That said, uncertainty isn't a reason for paralysis. One thing I find helpful is to separate what we can't know from what we simply haven't looked at carefully yet. We may not be able to predict what models will look like in ten years, but we can study the systems we have right now. That's a big part of why I care about interpretability and visualization. If we can see what's going on inside these models, how they represent the world, how they represent the person they're talking to, then we're not just guessing. We're building up real knowledge, and that knowledge tends to stay useful even as the technology changes.

The other piece is to keep people at the center. It's easy to talk about AI's effects in the abstract, in terms of benchmarks or GDP. But the effects land on actual individuals, on how they work, learn, and make decisions. So I think we should pay close attention to how people actually experience these tools, and design things so that people can understand them and push back when they need to. Transparency is not a complete answer, but it's a way of giving people some agency in the face of uncertainty, instead of asking them to simply trust that things will work out.

So: be humble about predictions, invest in understanding the systems we already have, and make sure the people affected have the tools and information to participate in shaping what happens next.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes real uncertainty, says respected people have repeatedly been surprised, and notes that we cannot predict what models will look like in ten years.

r002.rationale: It does not compare AI’s current stage to the early Industrial Revolution or steam engines.

r003.rationale: It does not frame navigating AI’s development and effects as a marathon or sustained undertaking.

r004.rationale: It recommends keeping people at the center and paying close attention to how they experience AI tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest starting point is to admit that we're really bad at this. If you look at the history of predictions about technology, the track record is humbling. People who were deeply expert in a field often got the big picture wrong, and sometimes outsiders got it right almost by accident. So the first move is a kind of epistemic humility, not as a rhetorical gesture but as an actual working principle.

What I find more useful than trying to predict is trying to see. A lot of my work has been about visualization, and the underlying idea there is that when you can't reason your way to an answer, sometimes you can look your way to one. With these models, we're in a strange position where we built them, but we don't really understand what's happening inside. So part of approaching uncertainty, for me, is investing in the instruments. Interpretability, probing, building tools that let people actually observe what a system is doing rather than just what it outputs. You reduce uncertainty not by arguing harder but by getting better measurements.

The second thing is to pay attention to effects on people at small scale before they're at large scale. The future of AI isn't just going to arrive one day. It's arriving in little pieces right now, in how a student writes an essay, how a radiologist reads a scan, how someone lonely talks to a chatbot at two in the morning. Those are observable. And I think there's a temptation to skip over them because they feel mundane compared to the grand narratives about superintelligence or mass unemployment. But the mundane stuff is where the evidence is.

And then I'd say, hold multiple scenarios in your head at once and design for more than one of them. If you're only preparing for the world where everything goes wonderfully, or only for the world where everything goes terribly, you'll be unprepared either way. The best engineering, and honestly the best policy, tends to be the stuff that's robust across the futures you can imagine, and that leaves room to correct course when you discover the future you didn't imagine.

I'd also just say, talk to people who aren't like you. The AI community has a particular way of seeing the world, and the people who'll be most affected by these systems are often not in the room. Uncertainty about effects on people is partly just a sampling problem. You can shrink it by widening who you listen to.

r001.rationale: The response stresses that predictions about technology are often wrong and recommends humility because AI’s effects remain uncertain.

r002.rationale: It does not compare AI’s current stage to the early Industrial Revolution or the first effective steam engines.

r003.rationale: It does not frame navigating AI’s development as a marathon or sustained undertaking.

r004.rationale: It recommends examining AI’s small-scale effects on people and listening to those most affected when assessing those effects.

astra-6.text:
I think we should start by being honest about what we don’t know. There’s a temptation to tell a very confident story about AI—either that everything is going to be wonderful or that everything is going to be terrible. And uncertainty doesn’t really justify either of those conclusions.

One useful approach is to make the questions more concrete. Which people are we talking about? What are they using the system for? Who gets to decide whether it’s working well? Something can be helpful to the person deploying it and harmful to the person on the receiving end.

So I’d want us to experiment, listen to the people affected, and build in ways to change course. We can study what’s happening now while keeping an open mind about what might happen next. You don’t have to predict the whole future to make a better decision today.

r001.rationale: The response stresses that we do not know the future and cautions against confident predictions about AI’s effects.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison to the early Industrial Revolution or steam engines.

r003.rationale: It does not frame AI’s development as a sustained undertaking or compare it to a marathon.

r004.rationale: It recommends experimenting, listening to affected people, and studying what is happening to understand AI’s effects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should start by being honest about how much we don’t know. There’s uncertainty about what these systems will be able to do, but also about how people will choose to use them. Those are different questions, and neither has a single inevitable answer.

One useful approach is to make the discussion concrete. Who is using a system? Who benefits? Who gets to challenge it when it makes a mistake? You can learn a lot by looking closely at those interactions, even if you can’t predict what AI will look like in ten years.

And uncertainty shouldn’t mean paralysis. It’s a reason to experiment carefully, listen to the people affected, and build in ways to change course. We should be skeptical of confident predictions, including our own, while still taking responsibility for the decisions we can make today.

r001.rationale: The response says we should be honest about how much we don’t know about AI’s future capabilities and how people will use it.

r002.rationale: It does not compare AI’s current stage to the early Industrial Revolution or steam engines.

r003.rationale: It does not frame navigating AI’s development as a sustained undertaking like a marathon.

r004.rationale: It recommends examining who uses AI, who benefits, and who is affected, and listening to those people when learning about its effects.
